summary: Specifies extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol so that a stateful PCE can compute and initiate Segment Routing traffic-engineering paths, and so a client can ask for a path with constraints and optimization criteria.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8664 lets a path-computation server send Segment Routing paths to routers using PCEP. It also lets routers report path limits and the segments they use.

questions: what is maximum sid depth in pcep
subtitle: PCEP extensions for computing and installing Segment Routing traffic-engineering paths.

tldr.problem: PCEP needs a way to carry Segment Routing paths and communicate the capabilities that determine which paths a router can use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8664 defines a Segment Routing path setup type, a capability message that includes maximum SID depth, and SR-ERO and SR-RRO subobjects for carrying and reporting segment lists.
tldr.outcome: Stateful PCEs can compute and initiate SR-TE paths, and PCCs can request them. RFC 8664 updates RFC 8408 and was updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933.

today: RFC 8664 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 8408 and has been updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs Segment Routing Support
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) represents a path as an ordered list of instructions called segments. In the MPLS forwarding plane covered here, segments are labels and an SR path corresponds to an MPLS Label Switching Path.

The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) connects a Path Computation Client (PCC) with a Path Computation Element (PCE). Existing stateful PCEP extensions let a PCE manage paths, but did not define all the SR-specific information required. This RFC adds extensions so a stateful PCE can compute and initiate SR traffic-engineering paths and a PCC can request an SR path from a stateful or stateless PCE.

The document relies on RFC 8408 for advertising the Segment Routing capability and identifying the path setup type. It also updates RFC 8408 to clarify how capability sub-TLVs are used.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE calculates a route and a PCC applies it. This RFC gives them PCEP messages for describing and requesting Segment Routing paths.

sections.title: How PCEP Carries an SR Path
sections.content:
In an SR network, the ingress node adds a list of Segment Identifiers (SIDs) to packets. For the MPLS data plane in this document, those SIDs are labels. The routing information distributed by the IGP helps guide packets along the path without a hop-by-hop signaling protocol.

PCEP carries route information in an Explicit Route Object (ERO), which is a sequence of subobjects. RFC 8664 defines an SR-ERO subobject that can carry a SID, the node or adjacency it identifies, or both. It also defines an SR-RRO subobject for a PCC to report the path it applied.

The extensions can also support changing an LSP between RSVP-TE and SR-TE. Resetting a PCEP session does not itself change established data-plane LSPs, and enabling the SR path setup type does not automatically move user traffic onto SR paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCE sends an ordered list of segments in an ERO. The PCC turns that list into labels for packets and can report the resulting path back to the PCE.

sections.title: Advertising SR Support and SID Depth
sections.content:
The RFC assigns Path Setup Type (PST) value 1 to Segment Routing. A PCEP speaker indicates support in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV in its OPEN object. If it advertises PST 1, it must also include the SR-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV, type 26 and length 4.

The capability sub-TLV includes an N flag, an X flag, and a Maximum SID Depth (MSD). The N flag says that a PCC can resolve a Node or Adjacency Identifier (NAI) to a SID. The X flag means there is no imposed MSD limit. Otherwise, MSD gives the maximum number of SIDs the PCC can add to a packet and must be greater than zero.

For an established session with a non-zero MSD, the PCE must not send a path with more SIDs than the limit. If the session uses MSD zero, the PCC may request a limit for an individual path computation with METRIC type 11. A PCE can use MSD information learned from routing protocols in preference to values in the capability sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Before exchanging paths, a PCC tells the PCE whether it can look up a node name and how many SIDs it can add to a packet. The PCE must keep each path within the advertised limit.

sections.title: The SR-ERO Subobject
sections.content:
An SR-ERO subobject carries a SID, a Node or Adjacency Identifier (NAI), or both. An ERO for an SR-TE path contains only SR-ERO subobjects. Their order defines the MPLS label stack: the first subobject gives the topmost label and the last gives the bottommost label.

The subobject has Type 36, a Length of at least 8 octets and a multiple of 4, an NAI Type field, flags, and optional SID and NAI values. The M flag says whether the SID value is an MPLS label stack entry or an index into the SRGB or SRLB. The S flag means the SID is absent and the PCC must resolve it from the NAI. The F flag means the NAI is absent. The C flag allows the PCE to specify traffic-class, bottom-of-stack, and TTL fields when M is set.

NAI Types identify an absent NAI, IPv4 or IPv6 node identifiers, or several forms of adjacency identifiers. The matching SR-RRO subobject reports the path without the ERO's L flag.
sections.plainLanguage: Each subobject identifies one segment by its SID, its node or adjacency identifier, or both. The order of the subobjects determines the order of labels that the PCC puts on packets.

sections.title: Validating and Applying the Path
sections.content:
A PCC checks the SR-ERO length and flags against the NAI Type. It rejects malformed subobjects, an ERO that mixes SR-ERO with other subobject types, or a list that mixes SID labels, indexes, and absent SIDs. It must not accept MPLS label value 3, which is Implicit NULL.

To apply a valid ERO, the PCC converts the subobjects to an MPLS label stack and a next hop, then adds the stack to packets sent along the path. It resolves index values using the SRGB or SRLB. If the ERO supplies only NAIs, the PCC looks up a matching prefix or adjacency with an associated SID.

If a SID, NAI, SRGB, or SRLB cannot be resolved, or if the path exceeds the PCC's SID limit, the PCC returns the specified PCErr. When an invalid ERO would change an existing LSP, the PCC must not update that LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCC checks that the path description is consistent and that each segment can be resolved. If the new route is invalid, it reports an error and does not replace an existing path.

sections.title: Choosing and Changing the Path Setup Type
sections.content:
SR can be used alongside other PCEP path setup types, including RSVP-TE. Both the PCC and PCE must advertise PST 1 and the SR-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV before they can use SR. A PCE can propose a setup type when it initiates an LSP; a PCC can nominate a preferred type when requesting a path. Local policy and node capabilities can affect the choice.

Implementations must let an operator enable or disable SR path setup and specify SR or RSVP-TE as a proposed or requested type. The migration procedure enables SR on PCEs and PCCs, then resets PCEP sessions. If a problem occurs, an operator can disable SR and reset sessions again. Established data-plane LSPs remain in place across a session reset.

Implementations should expose advertised capabilities and the path setup type used, and log capability mismatches or a different type selected than requested.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator enables SR at both ends of a PCEP session, then restarts the session to exchange the new capability. Existing paths remain in place during that reset.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the base PCEP and stateful PCEP specifications apply. The RFC says it requires no additional security measures, but describes two consequences if the PCEP session is not protected.

Because a controller can install a path without hop-by-hop signaling such as RSVP-TE, an attacker without session integrity protection could create a path that does not receive the checks performed by that signaling protocol. The MSD field also reveals how many MPLS labels a sender can add to a packet. Without strong encryption, this information may expose capabilities of edge devices.
sections.plainLanguage: An unprotected PCEP session could let an attacker install a path or learn a router's label-stack limit. The PCEP session needs the security protections described by the referenced base specifications.
